strengths: The core idea is interesting and timely: enabling fully differentiable, dense-vector communication between (stripped) LLMs via trainable seq2seq edge modules, moving beyond discrete-token multi-agent communication. This is a clean instantiation connecting 'LLM collectives' to differentiable training, related to but distinct from Coconut [13] and CommNet [37].

The scaling experiment (Table 1) is ambitious for the compute available: LMNet-1B, built from a shared Qwen2.5-0.5B with shared vertex weights, shows broad gains over the vertex model and competitive numbers against 1.5-3B open models on several benchmarks (e.g., BBH 47.3, MATH 38.8).

Two distinct application scenarios are evaluated: large-scale (re)pre-training and limited-data customization, with the latter compared against a reasonable set of PEFT baselines (LoRA, Prefix, Adapters) on E2E with sensible metrics, plus composed variants (LMNet+LoRA, +Prefix).

The paper includes useful secondary analyses: complexity analysis with vertex parameter sharing, attention visualizations across edges (Figure 3), and an honest failure to decode intermediate dense vectors, which candidly reports that the learned communication is not human-interpretable.
The main text is generally well organized, and the authors are explicit about their limited compute budget and that LMNet-1B is a proof of concept rather than a ready-to-use model.
weaknesses: The headline claim ('comparable performance with <0.1% training cost') lacks the decisive control experiment: continuing training of Qwen2.5-0.5B (or a simple depth-expanded variant, i.e., stacking copies of the model with adapters) on the same 0.01T tokens. Without this, it is impossible to attribute the gains to 'dense communication between LLMs' rather than to generic continued pre-training / depth growing of a single model. Notably, all vertices share one pre-trained LLM, so the 'communication between multiple LLMs' framing is only weakly instantiated in the main experiment.

Potential benchmark contamination undermines Table 1: the training mix explicitly includes MMLU (auxiliary split), MATH (train), and GSM8K (train), while the evaluation includes MMLU, MMLU-pro, MATH, and GSM8K. The baselines (Qwen/Llama/Gemma) were pre-trained without these benchmark training sets, making the 'less than 0.1% of training cost' comparison unfair. At minimum, results excluding benchmark-adjacent training data should be reported.

Proposition 1 is trivial (an application of the chain rule) and does not merit proposition status; claims such as the MLP universal-approximation analogy (Section 4.2) and the speculation in Section 4.4 about emergent collective intelligence are asserted without evidence.

Missing ablations for the central design choices: aggregation by summation, the fully-connected layer-wise topology vs. chain/tree alternatives, single-layer attention edges vs. alternatives, and edge parameter sharing. No error bars or variance reporting on any benchmark.

The customization results (Table 3) show LMNet losing to simple prompting on Qwen2.5-0.5B/1.5B on GSM8K, and the GSM8K results in 5.2.1 contain duplicated/contradictory explanatory sentences ('Second... Second...'), suggesting insufficient proofreading. Several grammatical issues ('a alternative', 'vertexes', 'does pass') appear throughout.

Reproducibility is limited: code is only promised ('will be released'), and key training details (learning rate, batch size, sequence length, optimizer, exact token counts per dataset) are omitted. Model merging and other training-free LLM-composition baselines, which are the natural competitors for combining existing LLMs, are neither discussed nor compared.

The 'collective intelligence' motivation (Society of Mind, Figure 1) oversells what is demonstrated: since all vertices are copies of one shared pre-trained model communicating through 1-layer attention blocks, the system is better described as a depth-expanded transformer with adapters, and the multi-model diversity angle (different LLMs per vertex) is never actually tested.

strengths: The core idea — direct dense-vector (continuous-space) communication between pre-trained LLMs with trainable seq2seq 'edge' modules, enabling fully differentiable end-to-end optimization of multi-model systems — is genuinely interesting and relatively underexplored compared to token-based multi-agent systems (only Coconut [13] and Sukhbaatar et al. [37] are identified as close relatives).

The scope of the empirical study is broad for a small compute budget: a 1.1B 're-pre-trained' LMNet evaluated across ~10 benchmarks, plus adaptation experiments on MMLU, GSM8K, and E2E against prompting, fine-tuning, and PEFT baselines, and a LoRA-integration variant showing the framework is composable.

Some self-critical analysis is present: the authors admit their de-embedding probe failed, acknowledge that strong backbone models gain little from LMNet (Tables 2–3), and state that the released LMNet-1B is a proof-of-concept rather than a ready-to-use artifact.

The formalization (stripping E/D layers, Eq. 1 layer-wise message passing, complexity analysis in 4.3) is simple and easy to follow, and parameter sharing across vertices makes the approach scalable in principle.
weaknesses: The headline claim — 'comparable performance with less than 0.1% training cost' — is misleading. The 0.01T-token budget excludes the pre-training of the vertex models (Qwen2.5-0.5B, trained on 18T tokens), and LMNet-1B has 2.3x the parameters of the vertex model. Reusing pre-trained weights amortized over the network's lifetime means the true compute accounting is far more favorable-looking than the '0.1%' framing suggests; the paper should report total amortized cost or reframe the claim.

A decisive control experiment is missing: simply continuing pre-training (or fine-tuning) the Qwen2.5-0.5B backbone on the same 0.01T-token mixture is never compared. Without this baseline, the observed gains cannot be attributed to dense inter-model communication rather than to additional training on a data mixture that includes MMLU auxiliary_training, GSM8K training, and MATH training splits.

Potential benchmark contamination undermines Table 1: LMNet-1B is trained on the training splits of MMLU, GSM8K, and MATH and then evaluated on the test splits of exactly those benchmarks, while the from-scratch baseline LLMs' exposure to these splits is not established or controlled. GSM8K/MATH gains (50.3 and 38.8 vs. baselines' much lower numbers) are the most likely to be inflated.

Inference cost is largely ignored. A forward pass requires L=5 sequential vertex applications plus ~34 edge modules per generated token (t = L*t_theta + L*W^2*t_omega per the paper's own analysis), i.e., roughly 5x the per-token latency of a single 1.1B model. Since deployment efficiency is a practical motivation, this materially weakens the 'efficiency' narrative, yet it is never discussed as a limitation.

Key architectural details needed for reproducibility are unspecified: how positional information is handled when multiple edge outputs (each of sequence length n) are summed into a pre-trained transformer that expects aligned positions, how KV caches work across layers, and standard training hyperparameters (optimizer, LR, batch size, sequence length) are all absent.

The analysis section is weak: the de-embedding probe failed, so the paper cannot show what information the edges transmit; the attention-weight visualization (Fig. 3) only shows edges 'pass different messages,' which is nearly tautological. Proposition 1 is just the chain rule and is oversold as a contribution.

Missing related work and baselines for 'combining pre-trained LLMs': knowledge distillation, model merging/soups, MoE with frozen experts, and modular deep learning approaches are natural competitors and are not discussed or compared; the related-work scope is limited to token-level multi-agent systems.

The customization results are mixed and not parameter-comparable: on Qwen backbones LMNet loses to simple prompting (Table 3), and in the E2E/PEFT comparison LMNet uses 21–141M trainable parameters versus LoRA's 0.35M, so beating LoRA there does not demonstrate parameter efficiency.

The writing contains numerous grammatical errors and at least one duplicated passage ('Second, these three LLMs are strong enough...' appears twice in Section 5.2.1), and there is no dedicated limitations section despite substantial scope restrictions (small scale, benchmark contamination risk, inference overhead).

strengths: The core idea—bypassing the embedding/de-embedding bottleneck to allow fully differentiable, dense-vector communication between pre-trained LLMs—is clean, well-motivated, and instantiated in a concrete, implementable framework (LMNet) with a clear formal specification (Section 3).

The empirical effort is non-trivial: a 1.14B-parameter system trained with a modest budget (<60 GPU-days), evaluated across ten standard benchmarks, plus a second application (customization with limited data) with sensible baselines (Pred/Prompt/FT/PEFT) where LMNet shows consistent gains (Tables 2-4).

Honest reporting of negative and inconclusive evidence, e.g., failing to decode intermediate dense representations, the GSM8K cases where LMNet loses to prompting (Table 3), and an explicit acknowledgment of limited compute rather than overselling the released model.

The paper correctly identifies the key differentiator versus prior multi-agent LLM systems: end-to-end differentiability enables gradient-based optimization of inter-model communication, which token-based pipelines cannot support.
weaknesses: The headline claim—'comparable performance with LLMs in similar size with only less than 0.1% training cost'—is confounded and not established. LMNet-1B builds on Qwen2.5-0.5B, which itself absorbed 18T pre-training tokens, while the comparison models (Llama3.2-1B, Qwen2.5-1.5B) were trained from scratch. Comparing only LMNet's additional 0.01T tokens against 15-18T from-scratch tokens does not support a 100x efficiency claim. The decisive missing control is continued pre-training of Qwen2.5-0.5B alone (or with trivial depth-stacking) on the same data mixture and budget; without it, gains cannot be attributed to dense communication rather than simply additional fine-tuning on a curated mixture.

Possible evaluation contamination: LMNet-1B's training mixture includes the GSM8K and MATH training splits and MMLU auxiliary training data, and the headline table (Table 1) reports test performance on these same benchmark families. The relationship between training data and evaluation for at least some reported numbers weakens the 'general intelligence' framing.

The 'similar size' comparison is selectively favorable: LMNet-1B trails Qwen2.5-1.5B on nearly every benchmark (MMLU 53.9 vs 60.9, GSM8K 50.3 vs 68.5, MMLU-stem 46.0 vs 54.8), yet the abstract and introduction emphasize comparability/superiority. A more defensible claim ('improves a given pre-trained model at modest cost') is buried in Section 5.1.1.

Analysis of how dense communication works is shallow: Proposition 1 is just the chain rule; the attempt to interpret intermediate messages failed; and the supporting evidence reduces to one case study and an attention-weight visualization (Figures 3-4) whose interpretive value is limited. Section 4.4's claims about 'emergent behaviors' and transcending component capabilities are asserted, not demonstrated.

Missing related work: the architecture—a single shared pre-trained LLM reused across depth with trained connector modules—closely resembles depth-recycling / recursive and looped-transformer lines (e.g., ALBERT-style sharing, Universal Transformer, recursive memory models) and continuous latent-space communication work beyond [13]; the paper does not position LMNet against these, weakening the novelty claim.

Presentation quality is below the bar for the main track: recurring grammatical errors ('many works combines', 'vertexes', 'cosider'), a duplicated sentence in Section 5.2.1 ('Second, these three LLMs are strong enough...' appears twice), and inconsistent claims (Section 5.1.1 says edge modules are 'to be optimized' before describing training). Hyperparameters, training schedules, and data quantities are under-specified for reproducibility (code is only promised).

strengths: Clear and well-motivated framing: recasting multi-model LLM systems as 'language model networks' organized by topology, communication medium, and optimization provides a useful unifying lens over TTS, multi-agent systems, workflow search, and latent reasoning.

LMNet is a clean, concrete instantiation: stripping embedding/de-embedding layers from intermediate LLMs and inserting trainable seq2seq edge modules makes inter-model communication dense and fully differentiable, enabling end-to-end training without supervising intermediate messages.

Breadth of empirical evaluation: two distinct application settings (general capability improvement and limited-supervision adaptation), multiple backbones (GPT2-XL, GPT2-M, Llama3.2-1B, Qwen2.5-0.5B/1.5B/3B/7B), comparisons against prompting, SFT, TTS (Self-Refine/Self-Consistency), latent reasoning (COCONUT, CODI), and PEFT methods, plus ablations on depth/width and integration with PEFT (Tables 5, 6, 11).

The authors candidly discuss what the method is and is not: Section 6.3 admits the gain comes from added test-time computation with repurposed vertices rather than literal sentence-by-sentence message passing, the limitations section discusses cost, interpretability, and access requirements, and Appendix C transparently reports settings where LMNet fails.

Parameter sharing across vertices and lightweight edge modules (Section 3.3) makes the complexity analysis concrete; total training cost (<0.2% of pre-training, <100 GPU-days) is reasonable for the claims made.
weaknesses: The central 'learned communication' narrative is weakened by the paper's own evidence. Figure 3 shows most intermediate vertices de-embed to 'Same as Final Answer', and Appendix B.1 finds no meaningful edge-level structure ('fully exploited... without distinguishable substructures'). Combined with Section 6.3's admission, the system behaves more like a deeper, wider stack of the same LLM than an emergent communication network; the framing overstates what is demonstrated.

Baseline fairness and scale of gains are concerns. Gains shrink substantially on stronger backbones (e.g., Table 2: Qwen2.5-1.5B LMNet 37.28 vs Prompt 35.83; Table 9: LMNet 30.93 vs Prompt 41.60 on Qwen2.5-0.5B GSM8K), suggesting most of the benefit appears on weak models and may largely reflect extra capacity/compute per token rather than communication. A depth-matched or width-matched single-model baseline (e.g., finetuning a 1.1B model, or deeper continuous-depth variants) is missing from the main comparison.

Data contamination risk for the general-capability experiments: the paper itself notes the training data 'is likely to be seen during the pre-training of LLM', and training uses the MMLU auxiliary split, GSM8K/MATH training sets while evaluating on exactly those benchmarks; the claimed +30.5% general improvement needs stronger controls to be interpretable as capability gain.

Mechanistic and design details that determine reproducibility are under-specified in the main text: how positional information is handled for edge-transformer inputs, KV-cache management across 14 repeated vertex applications, choice and tuning of Agg, and why sum aggregation with a shared causal mask is valid when messages are summed into another model's stream. Much relies on appendices.

Novelty is moderate: latent-space communication between LLM modules (COCONUT, CODI, compressed CoT, learned workflow graphs like GPTSwarm) already exists; the contribution is mainly a specific architecture (fully connected layer-wise topology + attention-block edges) and the honest conceptual framing, which the authors themselves partially walk back in Section 6.3.

Some statistical rigor is missing: no error bars, seeds, or variance reporting across the many benchmark numbers, and several ablations (Table 6 depth/width) show 'no significant difference', leaving the topology hypothesis weakly validated.

strengths: The 'language model network' framing is an interesting and reasonably coherent lens that unifies test-time scaling, multi-agent workflows, and latent reasoning as design choices over node function, communication medium, and topology.

The core mechanism is clearly specified: stripping embedding/de-embedding layers between model nodes, inserting trainable seq2seq edge modules, and using a layer-wise fully-connected topology makes the inter-model communication path fully differentiable and end-to-end trainable from final task supervision alone.

Empirical coverage is broad for the scale attempted: general capability improvement on 11 benchmarks (Table 1), multi-backbone experiments on MMLU/GSM8K (Tables 2, 3), the standard E2E/PEFT benchmark (Table 4), model-size ablations (Table 5), and integration with PEFT methods (Table 11).

The limitations section and Section 6.3 are unusually honest: the authors acknowledge that the current end-to-end auto-regressive implementation does not actually realize sentence-level message passing, that intermediate messages are not semantically readable, and that dense communication requires access to model internals, which is a fair characterization of the gap between the motivating vision and the realized method.

The qualitative analysis in Appendix B (de-embedding intermediate outputs, showing early vertices producing compact intermediate information) is a genuine attempt to open the black box of learned communication.
weaknesses: The paper's own concessions undercut its central narrative. Section 6.3 admits the implementation 'does not exactly match the image of replacing inefficient NL messages' and that gains 'should be attributed to more test-time computation.' Combined with Appendix B.2 (inputs to intermediate vertices are not even English-like), the evidence supports 'a deeper network with extra modules' more than 'learned communication.' The framing oversells what was built.

The most important baseline is missing: fine-tuning a single model of comparable total size (e.g., a ~1.1B model, or Qwen2.5-0.5B widened/deepened with extra layers) on the same data. The paper dismisses comparison with similar-size pretrained LLMs as 'not fair,' but that comparison is precisely what would disentangle 'learned communication' from 'more parameters and more compute on top of a good initialization.'

Contamination is not adequately addressed. LMNet is trained on the auxiliary/training splits of MMLU, MATH, and GSM8K and then evaluated on those same benchmarks, while baseline pretrained models are evaluated zero/few-shot on data they may not have been optimized for. The claim that LMNet's benefit 'comes from the learned communication rather than the training data' rests on SFT being surprisingly weak (-5.7%), which may simply reflect under-tuned SFT ('very moderate training configurations'); no evidence is given that SFT was carefully tuned.

Compute-matched comparisons are crude: matching LMNet's 14 vertex passes plus 0.6B edge parameters to Self-Refine/Self-Consistency at ×16 trials is a rough equivalence, and latency/cost accounting (L×tθ + L×W²×tω) is asserted rather than measured.

Scale and rigor limits: all headline experiments use 0.5B vertices, no seeds/variance/significance testing are reported, ablations are confined to small-scale tasks, and the GSM8K results in Appendix C/Table 9 show the method actually fails against prompting for some backbones—an inconsistency that is explained post hoc rather than resolved.

Novelty is moderate: the combination of parameter-shared repeated backbone, learned per-edge adapters, and dense vector handoff is closely related to depth-recycled/looped transformers, latent reasoning (COCONUT, CODI), and cooperative LM work; the paper differentiates mostly by topology, which its own ablations (Table 6, Appendix B.1) show yields 'no significant difference or patterns.'

Presentation issues: the code link in Section 4 is empty ('Code is provided at .'), Appendix B's macro-level 'analysis' amounts to inspecting heatmap statistics and concluding no pattern exists, and the paper contains numerous grammatical and notational rough edges (e.g., 'a alternative', 'Specially', loose notation in Section 3.1).

strengths: The paper articulates a coherent and timely framing of multi-model LLM systems as 'language model networks' and identifies the discrete-token communication bottleneck and its supervision/optimization consequences clearly.

The proposed construction (stripped transformers as vertices, trainable seq2seq edge modules, single embedding/de-embedding at the system boundary) is simple, well-motivated, and genuinely end-to-end differentiable, preserving the natural-language I/O interface.

The evaluation is unusually broad for this kind of system paper: two application settings, multiple backbones (GPT2, GPT2-M, Llama3.2-1B, Qwen2.5-0.5B/1.5B/3B/7B), multiple benchmark families, comparisons against prompting, SFT, TTS (Self-Refine, Self-Consistency), latent reasoning (COCONUT, CODI), and PEFT baselines on the standard E2E/LoRA protocol.

The limitations discussion is candid and specific: the authors acknowledge in Section 6.3 that the end-to-end auto-regressive implementation does not realize the motivating picture of sentence-level message passing, that gains should partly be attributed to extra test-time computation, and that dense communication requires model-internal access and sacrifices interpretability.

Appendix C honestly reports failure cases (LMNet underperforming Prompt on Qwen models with small GSM8K training data), and the ablations over depth/width and vertex model size add useful, if limited, evidence.
weaknesses: The central causal claim — that 'learned communication' rather than extra parameters and compute drives the gains — is not convincingly disentangled. There is no natural ablation isolating the contribution of the learned edge modules, e.g., a compute-matched configuration with frozen/random or identity edges, or a simple residual-stacking of the same backbone without the network framing. Section 6.3 essentially concedes the gains 'should be attributed to more test-time computation, where each vertex has been equipped with some newly assigned function,' which undermines the headline narrative.

The SFT baseline in Table 1 is described as using 'very moderate training configurations' and yields -5.7% relative improvement, which makes the +30.5% headline comparison fragile. Similarly, no equal-FLOP baseline (e.g., continued pre-training of Qwen2.5-0.5B with the same 0.02T-token budget) is provided to substantiate the '<0.2% of pre-training cost' efficiency claim.

Potential data contamination is acknowledged ('this public data is likely to be seen during the pre-training of LLM') but not resolved; the very large jumps on BBH (20.3→47.3) and MATH (19.5→38.8) warrant stronger evidence that the improvement is a property of the architecture rather than memorization.

Novelty positioning relative to the closest line of work is incomplete. Recurrent-depth/latent-iteration methods that repeatedly apply the same backbone with learned latent interfaces (e.g., Geiping et al.'s recurrent depth, beyond COCONUT/CODI) are not discussed, even though LMNet with vertex parameter sharing is closely related to them; the differentiation is thinner than the related-work section suggests.

The analysis of learned communication (Appendix B) is weak: the macro-level analysis concludes 'no significant pattern' from parameter-matrix visualizations, and the micro-level analysis is a single case study. The claim that the fully connected topology is 'fully exploited' is not well supported.

Reproducibility is compromised: the code link in Section 4 is empty, key training details are deferred to an appendix that remains thin on hyperparameters, and several ablations are confined to the small GPT2-M scale, limiting confidence in scaling behavior.

The ablation in Table 6 shows no significant architecture patterns, and the paper's topology hypothesis (fully connected, universal-approximation-inspired) is asserted rather than validated; alternative topologies, aggregation functions (concatenation vs. sum), and routing are discussed but not tested.

Writing quality is uneven: grammatical errors ('a alternative', 'between LMNet between them', 'formulate'), an ambiguous empty code URL, and four appendix figures of near-uniform green heatmaps that convey little information.
